newsitem.title: USA: U.S. oil independents' output seen growing - IPAA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oil independents' output seen growing - IPAA.

text.p: U.S. independent oil producers has grown to 40 percent of domestic oil production, up from about 31 percent 10 years ago, according to data from the Independent Petroleum Association of America (IPAA).
At an investors conference in New York Wednesday, IPAA's chairman Lew Ward said smaller producers' share of natural gas output was at 66 percent from about 58 percent in 1987.

"I am pleased to be here on behalf of America's oil and gas producers who are responsible for 66 percent of the nation's natural gas production and 40 percent of the crude oil," he told executives at an IPAA meeting Wednesday.
"There is a 'can-do' attitude among people in our business," Ward told a luncheon at the IPAA Oil and Gas Investment Symposium here.

Earlier, the group released its domestic supply and demand forecasts, which included the surprising prediction that U.S. production levels would actually expand marginally for the first time since 1984 through the year 2000.
IPAA said the three percent annual declines seen since 1985 would flatten out, and that 1997 would see crude output rise by 21,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 6.5 million bpd.
"What's driving the increase?" Ward said. "Stronger prices coupled with improvements in technology and rising activity in the offshore."
IPAA also said domestic demand that outpaces the output increases would be met by increased imports, which by the year 2000 will expand to 55 percent from 53 percent this year.
"Another development that could soon stimulate production is Alaska's eagerness to draw more producing companies to its state," Ward said.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk, 1 212 859 1633
